newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Airlines formalise alliance, seek partners.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Airlines formalise alliance, seek partners.

text.p: A group of major airlines, including Deutsche Lufthansa AG and United Airlines, on Wednesday formally branded their existing partnership with the name "Star Alliance" but said no merger would take place.
The alliance, in addition to Lufthansa and United, includes Air Canada, Scandinavian Airlines Systems and Thai Airways International Ltd.
Other airlines are expected to join the expanding group, including confirmation on Wednesday that Brazil's Varig Airlines will join in October.
The partners said other potential partners include South African Airways and regional European carrier British Midland, which both now cooperate with Lufthansa.
Talks were also being held with unnamed Asian airlines to strengthen the alliance's presence in the expanding region but alliance airline executives declined further comment.
But the airlines, who have been working closely together for a few years, said they would not take equity stakes in one another and each airline would retain its individual identity.

"It is not our intention to merge our airlines nor to develop identical product offerings. Our research tells us categorically that our customers enjoy and appreciate our varied cultures," the airlines said in a statement.

The branding deal, a bid to cut costs and offer integrated "same airline" travel for passengers and cargo, creates one of the largest industry alliances and rivals that announced last year by British Airways and American Airlines.
The five airlines, dubbed "The airline network for Earth", have a combined staff of more than 210,000 employees and flights to 578 cities in 106 countries.

The alliance airlines showed off the power of their size, saying their combined revenues in 1996 would have totalled $42.3 billion and they would have carried about 174 million passengers on flights around the world.
The partners projected annual global passenger growth of five to six percent in the coming years and Lufthansa said cargo shipment growth would average six to seven percent.
The partnership calls for common branding in marketing and advertising and to intensify, when possible, coordination of routes and the offering of code-share flights, where
Passengers will also be able to accumulate and redeem mileage points on any of the partner airlines and for further integration of some airport operations, purchasing and ticketing operations.

"The Star Alliance brand will provide a mark of quality and benefits, including worldwide recognition. The brand name will compliment - but not replace - each airline's individual identity and product offerings in their home markets and around the world," the airlines said in the statement.
The airlines, in a joint statement a news conference at Frankfurt Airport, also said they did not expect the partnership to violate regulatory anti-competition laws.
"The Star Alliance poses no threat to competition and provides distinct customer benefits," the airlines said.

The carriers noted anti-trust immunity already exists for the relationship between United, Lufthansa and SAS in the United States and immunity for United's alliance with Air Canada is pending among regulatory authorities.
The European Union is still investigating the alliance, but the carriers said in the statement that they did not expect any problems from the review by Brussels.
